Experimental design and analysis for tree improvement

Dongwen Luo

Source: vignettes/articles/tree-improvement.Rmd
tree-improvement.Rmd

This article gives R code for the worked examples of the book Experimental Design and Analysis for Tree Improvement (Williams, Harwood and Matheson, 2023). The data sets come with the package eda4treeR (Yaseen et al., 2023). Each example follows the book: the data, the model, a check of the residuals, the analysis of variance and the predicted means with their pairwise comparisons, computed with predictmeans. Section titles give the book’s example number and page. Where the analysis here differs from the book’s, the text says why. The code of each step is folded: click Code to see it.

Mixed models are fitted with lme4::lmer() (attached with predictmeans). Their F tests (anova()) and predicted means use Kenward-Roger standard errors and degrees of freedom, as SAS PROC MIXED DDFM=KR (Kenward and Roger, 1997); variance components are from varcomp().

Code 
library(tidyverse)
library(predictmeans)
library(eda4treeR)
library(gridExtra)
library(car)
library(DT)
library(gt)
library(summarytools)
library(knitr)

2.1 Example 2.1 (Pg. 24)

A field trial was planted to compare a seedlot derived from a seed orchard (SO) with one collected from a routine plantation (P). There were eight plots of each seedlot, thinned at seven years of age. Tree diameters at breast height (dbh) were measured at 15 years and plot means calculated.

Data Info

Code 
data(DataExam2.1, package="eda4treeR")
str(DataExam2.1)
## 'data.frame':    16 obs. of  2 variables:
##  $ seedlot: Factor w/ 2 levels "SO","P": 1 1 1 1 1 1 1 1 2 2 ...
##  $ dbh    : num  30.4 27.9 28.1 31.4 30.1 ...
Code 
print(dfSummary(DataExam2.1, 
                varnumbers   = FALSE, 
                valid.col    = FALSE, 
                graph.magnif = 0.76),
      method = 'render')

2026-11-25

Code 
DataExam2.1 %>% 
  ggplot(aes(x=seedlot, y=dbh, col=seedlot, fill=seedlot))+
  geom_boxplot(width=0.3, alpha=0.4)+

Modelling

Code 
fmtab2.3 <- lm(formula = dbh ~ seedlot , data = DataExam2.1)
summary(fmtab2.3)
## 
## Call:
## lm(formula = dbh ~ seedlot, data = DataExam2.1)
## 
## Residuals:
##     Min      1Q  Median      3Q     Max 
## -3.0725 -0.9200 -0.2769  0.9887  3.8975 
## 
## Coefficients:
##             Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
## (Intercept)  30.5813     0.7405  41.300 4.98e-16 ***
## seedlotP     -1.8888     1.0472  -1.804   0.0928 .  
## ---
## Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1
## 
## Residual standard error: 2.094 on 14 degrees of freedom
## Multiple R-squared:  0.1886, Adjusted R-squared:  0.1306 
## F-statistic: 3.253 on 1 and 14 DF,  p-value: 0.09284
Code 
residplot(fmtab2.3)

Code 
#perform shapiro-wilk test
shapiro.test(resid(fmtab2.3))
## 
##  Shapiro-Wilk normality test
## 
## data:  resid(fmtab2.3)
## W = 0.95485, p-value = 0.5701
Code 
#perform bartlett test
bartlett.test(dbh ~ seedlot , data = DataExam2.1)
## 
##  Bartlett test of homogeneity of variances
## 
## data:  dbh by seedlot
## Bartlett's K-squared = 0.20322, df = 1, p-value = 0.6521
Code 
#perform levene test 
car::leveneTest(dbh ~ seedlot , data = DataExam2.1)
## Levene's Test for Homogeneity of Variance (center = median)
##       Df F value Pr(>F)
## group  1  0.0135 0.9091
##       14

ANOVA

Code 
kable(anova(fmtab2.3), digits = 4)
Df Sum Sq Mean Sq F value Pr(>F)
seedlot 1 14.2695 14.2695 3.2531 0.0928
Residuals 14 61.4098 4.3864 NA NA

Predicted Means

Code 
predm_out <- predictmeans(fmtab2.3, "seedlot", meandecr=TRUE, adj="BH")
print(predm_out[1:4])
## $`Predicted Means`
## seedlot
##      SO       P 
## 30.5813 28.6925 
## 
## $`Standard Error of Means`
## All means have the same SE 
##                    0.74047 
## 
## $`Standard Error of Differences`
##  Max.SED  Min.SED Aveg.SED 
## 1.047189 1.047189 1.047189 
## 
## $LSD
##  Max.LSD  Min.LSD Aveg.LSD 
##    2.246    2.246    2.246 
## attr(,"Significant level")
## [1] 0.05
## attr(,"Degree of freedom")
## [1] 14
## attr(,"Note")
## [1] "These LSDs are not adjusted: 'BH' is a step-wise method and has no critical value for all pairs. Use the adjusted p-values for the comparisons."
## attr(,"equal")
## [1] TRUE
Code 
gt(predm_out$mean_table$Table, 
   caption = "Group: Letter-based representation of pairwise comparisons at significant level '0.05'")
Group: Letter-based representation of pairwise comparisons at significant level '0.05'
seedlot Mean SE Df LL(95%) UL(95%) LetterGrp
SO 30.5813 0.74047 14 28.9931 32.1694 A
P 28.6925 0.74047 14 27.1043 30.2807 A
Code 
autoplot(predm_out)
Code 
autoplot(predm_out, type = "ci", data = TRUE)
Code 
autoplot(predm_out, type = "bar")

3.1 Example 3.1 (Pg. 30)

We illustrate the recommended layout for data sheets with one of the trials conducted by the Australian Centre for International Agricultural Research (ACIAR) in Queensland, Australia (Experiment 309). This was a species trial planted in 1985; survival was poor. For our example we will examine only part of the data from this experiment. Five of the species with good survival have been extracted at random, namely Acacia, Angophora, Casuarina, Melaleuca and Petalostigma.

Code

## 'data.frame':    80 obs. of  6 variables:

4.1 Example 4.3 (Pg. 53)

Data Info

Major seed distributors such as the Australian Tree Seed Centre (ATSC) routinely conduct seed viability tests so that, when seed is dispatched, the purchaser has an indication of the germination percentage of the seed. As part of the ATSC research program, a series of experiments was conducted in 1992 by Debbie Solomon on provenances of Acacia mangium to investigate methods of pre-treatment and loss of viability of stored seed. Each experiment involved six seedlots of Acacia mangium and four seed pre-treatments in a factorial design with three replicates.

4.2 Example 4.4 (Pg. 61)

Data Info

An experiment supported by the Shell Company was planted at Toolara Forest Reserve near Gympie, Queensland, in February 1987 to study the effects of irrigation and fertiliser on four seedlots of Eucalyptus grandis. Because of the difficulty in applying the irrigation and fertiliser treatments individually to each 7 × 6 plot of trees, the experiment was designed as a split-plot, with main-plot treatments, irrig and fert. There were two replicates of four main-plots each with four sub-plots.

5.2 Example 5.1 (Pg. 68)

Data Info

In 1985 species/provenance trials were laid out at six sites in Thailand as part of an ACIAR project extending over several years to investigate Australian multi-purpose tree species. The experimental design in each case was an RCB design with three replicates and the number of seedlots ranged from 30 to 42. Plots consisted of 5 × 5 trees with a 2m × 2m spacing. Plot summary files were constructed for the 24-month measurement according to the methods described in Chapter 3. Analyses were performed on the plot mean data at each site.

  • Table of seedlot mean and regression coefficients

Site means absorb the main slope on sitemean (it is constant within a site), so the model estimates only the differences between the seedlots’ slopes (sitemean:seedlot). As in joint regression analysis, the slopes are scaled to average 1. For this complete table they equal the book’s Table 5.7.

Code 
predm_seedlot <- predictmeans(mod_5.1, "seedlot", plot=FALSE)$mean_table
d <- c(0, coef(mod_5.1)[grep("^sitemean:seedlot", names(coef(mod_5.1)))])   # slope differences from the first seedlot
predm_seedlot$reg_coef <- 1 + d - mean(d)
gt(predm_seedlot)

  • Table of seedlot mean and regression coefficients

Site means absorb the main slope on sitemean (it is constant within a site), so the model estimates only the differences between the seedlots’ slopes (sitemean:seedlot). As in joint regression analysis, the slopes are scaled to average 1. With the incomplete table the model adjusts each slope for the sites the seedlot was not grown at, so they differ a little from the separate regressions of Table 5.9.

Code 
predm_seedlotN <- predictmeans(mod_5.2, "seedlot", plot=FALSE)$mean_table
d <- c(0, coef(mod_5.2)[grep("^sitemean:seedlot", names(coef(mod_5.2)))])   # slope differences from the first seedlot
predm_seedlotN$reg_coef <- 1 + d - mean(d)
gt(predm_seedlotN)

Heritability

Narrow-sense heritability of a single tree: the additive variance is the family variance divided by the coefficient of relationship among members of an open-pollinated family, taken as 0.3 in the book (between half-sibs, 0.25, and full-sibs, 0.5). Plot means hold only 1/n of the variance among trees within a plot, so the single-tree variance needs that variance (within_variance) and the number of trees per plot (within_n, harmonic mean): σP2=σf2+σm2+σw2\sigma^2_P = \sigma^2_f + \sigma^2_m + \sigma^2_w, with plot variance σm2=σe2−σw2/n\sigma^2_m = \sigma^2_e - \sigma^2_w/n.

Code 
heritability(fm6.3.1, "Family", method = "family", relationship = 0.3,
             within_variance = "Dbh.variance", within_n = "Dbh.count")
## Narrow-sense heritability of a single plant (relationship 0.3) (95% limits)
## Variance of Family 0.2584; residual 1.167; within plots 3.921 (4.41 plants per plot)
## 
##  method estimate std.error conf.low conf.high
##  family   0.1933   0.09276  0.07393    0.4772

The heritability of family means (the precision of the family ranking in this trial). The data are balanced, so the standard, Cullis, Piepho and Oakey forms agree; the mean reliability is a little lower (it leaves out the covariances of the prediction errors), and the simulated form differs by its Monte Carlo error (printed below the table).

Code 
heritability(fm6.3.1, "Family", method = "all", seed = 1)
## Heritability on a line-mean basis (95% limits)

With all three provenances, provenance is a fixed effect, so the family variance is that within provenances.

Code 
fm6.4.1 <- lmer(Dbh.mean ~ Replication + Province + (1 | Family), data = DataExam6.2)
gt(varcomp(fm6.4.1), rownames_to_stub = TRUE)

8.1 Example 8.1 (Pg. 139)

Data Info

In the early 1990s Khongsak Pinyopusarerk of CSIRO Forestry and Forest Products initiated a far-reaching study of Casuarina equisetifolia. This is a nitrogen-fixing tree of considerable social, economic and environmental importance in tropical/subtropical littoral zones of Asia, the Pacific and Africa. Provenance collections were obtained from 18 countries and, with this material, more than 40 trials were laid out in 20 countries. The number of seedlots included in each trial varied, depending on the suitability and size of the planting sites for the available material. One of the trials, in Weipa, northern Queensland, contained all the available seedlots and is the example used here.

Modelling

Inoculation was applied to whole replicates, so it is tested in the replicate stratum (2 df). Each row-by-column position within a replicate is one plot, the residual unit, so Error(repl) gives the two strata (Error(repl/(row:col)) adds a stratum that is the residual itself). The means and SEDs below are computed by strata and agree with Genstat.

Code 
fm8.2 <- aov(dbh ~ inoc*(country/prov) + Error(repl), data = DataExam8.1)

8.5 Example 8.2 (Pg. 157)

Data Info

In Example 7.1 we discussed a Eucalyptus clone trial conducted in Vietnam and described the experimental layout. The trial tested 56 hybrid clones of the interspecific hybrid combination E. urophylla × E. pellita (UP). These candidates had been selected from progeny trials of control-pollinated hybrid families; here we ignore the parental origins of the different UP clones.

Modelling

Clone effects are random for the test clones only (contcompf = 1); the four standards are fixed effects (contcompf:standard). This is Genstat’s contcompv.clone with contcompv = 1 for test clones and 0 for standards. (1 | contcompv:clone) would instead add one more random “clone” holding all 20 standard plots (their clone is "0"), confounded with the fixed contcompf effect: it changes the test of contcompf (F 4.8 on 43 df instead of 73 on 255).

Code 
fm8.7 <- lmer(dbh ~ repl + column + contcompf + contcompf:standard + (1 | repl:row) + (1 | repl:column) +
                (0 + dummy(contcompf, "1") | clone), data = DataExam8.2)
summary(fm8.7, corr=FALSE)

ANOVA, adjusted R2R^2, Varcomp

  • ANOVA

Sequential (Type I) tests with Kenward-Roger df, = SAS PROC MIXED (HTYPE=1, DDFM=KR). Genstat’s “sequentially adding terms” tests the same hypotheses for repl and contcompf.standard and different ones for column and contcompf, because it builds them from the fitted variances; it also uses an F without Kenward-Roger’s adjustment (see ?anova.lmerMod). Genstat’s Wald and F statistics:
